title: Britannia, Bikano, and Beyond: Indian Snack Brands Storm the American Grocery Aisle
excerpt: From Walmart's $10 billion India sourcing pledge to Truly Indian's 1,300-store blitz, packaged Indian food is carving out shelf space that restaurants alone never could.
body:
For decades, the only place most Indian Americans could find Bourbon chocolate cream biscuits, Bikano namkeen, or proper chai masala was at a Patel Brothers, a Raja Foods outlet, or — in a pinch — a friend's suitcase fresh off a Mumbai flight. That geography is shifting fast.

Walmart, the world's largest retailer, has announced an aggressive expansion of Indian food sourcing for its US stores as part of a broader pledge to import $10 billion worth of goods from India annually by 2027. The new product lineup includes household names that will make NRI hearts skip: **Britannia's** Bourbon biscuits, Good Day cookies, and classic Milk Rusk; **Bikano's** festive packs featuring traditional savouries, mixtures, and sweets like Soan Papdi and Gulab Jamun; and spices from **Jayanti Spices**. Brands like Regal Kitchen and Vahdam tea are already on Walmart shelves.

Indian food, it turns out, has outgrown the specialty aisle.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

Indian cuisine is now the **second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America**, according to research firm Datassential. The broader US ethnic food market stands at an estimated $24.5 billion, and Indian food's share of that pie is accelerating faster than almost any other segment.

Consider the trajectory of **Truly Indian**, a CPG brand backed by ADF Foods, one of India's oldest food manufacturers (founded 1932). Since launching in the US market in May 2024, Truly Indian has expanded to more than 1,300 stores nationwide, offering frozen samosas handmade in India, low-glycemic tandoori naan baked in traditional clay ovens, high-protein roti wraps positioned as "India's answer to the burrito," and plant-based frozen entrées using coconut and cashew-based dairy alternatives.

Then there is **Gymkhana Fine Foods**, which landed at Whole Foods stores nationally this week. Born from London's two-Michelin-starred Gymkhana restaurant — operated by the Sethi siblings' JKS group, which boasts eight Michelin stars across its portfolio — the brand's simmer sauces and marinades are priced between $8 and $10 and designed to deliver a restaurant-quality meal in under thirty minutes. The launch came with an $8.5 million Series A led by CAVU Consumer Partners, co-founded by "Shark Tank" investor Rohan Oza.

## Why Now?

Several forces have converged to create this moment. First, the Indian-American population has crossed five million and is the highest-earning ethnic group in the United States, giving brands a reliable, premium-paying base consumer. Second, non-Indian American consumers have become dramatically more adventurous. Technomic data shows 52 percent of American consumers have tried Indian food and liked it. Third, the supply chain has matured: Indian manufacturers can now meet American food safety standards, labeling requirements, and cold-chain logistics at scale.

But perhaps the most important shift is perceptual. Indian food is no longer being positioned as "ethnic" or "exotic." Gymkhana's sauces sit in the same aisle as Rao's marinara and Trader Joe's simmer sauces — not in a segregated international foods section. Truly Indian's frozen samosas compete directly with Amy's and Sweet Earth in the natural frozen case. The framing has changed from "try this strange foreign thing" to "here is a better version of what you already buy."

## The Desi Kitchen Paradox

For the Indian diaspora, this mainstreaming triggers a complicated set of emotions. There is genuine excitement at seeing familiar brands on American shelves — a kind of cultural arrival that goes deeper than restaurant awards or celebrity chefs. When your mother's Bourbon biscuits are at Walmart, India has made it in a way that a Michelin star, however prestigious, does not quite capture.

But there is also anxiety. Will mass-market versions of Indian food flatten its extraordinary regional diversity into a lowest-common-denominator "curry"? Will Gymkhana's $9 Butter Masala sauce taste anything like what the Sethis serve at their London original? Will Walmart's Bikano Soan Papdi carry the same magic as the box a visiting uncle brought from Chandni Chowk?

These are not idle questions. The history of ethnic food in America — from Italian to Chinese to Mexican — suggests that mainstream adoption always involves some simplification. The question is whether Indian food's extraordinary range, from Chettinad to Kashmiri to Konkani, can survive the American grocery aisle's demand for legibility and ease.

## What Is Next

The pace is only accelerating. Walmart's India sourcing executive Andrea Albright has framed the push as bringing "a taste of India's rich culture and traditions to our customers in the US during the holiday season and beyond." Truly Indian's parent company, ADF Foods, is expanding its distribution across e-commerce and quick commerce. And London-based Dishoom, buoyed by an L Catterton investment, is reportedly developing a US retail line of its own.

For the first time, an NRI in Omaha or Boise or Tallahassee can stock a reasonably authentic Indian pantry without driving to the nearest metro's Little India. Whether that pantry produces a dal that would make an Indian grandmother nod with approval is another matter entirely.

But the shelf space has been won. And in the story of Indian food in America, that might be the chapter that mattered most.
